articles.title: A new cancer drug costs as much as a home down payment each month. Doctors say that's greed, not health care
articles.summary: Vancouver's James Howard is paying $90,000 a month for a new pancreatic cancer treatment that may add a few more months to his life. But, he's far from the only Canadian who is faced with having to…

image.caption: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the drug daraxonrasib to treat pancreatic cancer in August, but it's not yet approved in Canada. That means Canadian patients who want access to the medicine may have to pay tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket to access it. (Danielle Villasana/Re

blocks.text: James Howard thinks most people would say they're willing to pay any price to stay alive — until they're asked to put a dollar figure on it.
"The question that nobody's ever prepared to ask themselves is how much is your life worth ... and how long does that decision take for you," he said.
For Howard, the answer is $90,000 a month for a new pancreatic cancer drug he hopes will extend his life.
Doctors in Vancouver diagnosed Howard with pancreatic cancer in November 2025. He underwent chemotherapy, but the cancer has since metastasized and is now Stage 4.

Earlier this year, he learned about daraxonrasib, a treatment approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August but not yet in Canada. At three doses a day, it costs him about $63,000 US — roughly $90,000 Cdn — a month.

Howard is far from the only Canadian confronting the soaring cost of new cancer treatments. Oncologists across the country say increasingly expensive drugs — particularly treatments not yet approved or publicly funded in Canada — are forcing some patients to choose between paying enormous sums themselves and going without potentially life-extending medication.

James Howard, seen in his Vancouver home, takes three doses per day of the new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, which isn't approved in Canada and that he has to get from the U.S. at a cost of about $90,000 Cdn. a month. (Glen Kugelstadt/CBC News)
More than two dozen cancer specialists who spoke with CBC News said the trend is putting growing pressure on patients and the public health-care system.
It's not that pharmaceutical companies don't deserve to make money from their products, says Dr. Christopher Booth, a medical oncologist in Kingston, Ont.
But he says prices have reached a point where profit can come at the expense of patients.
"Corporate greed is gonna harm patients and health systems," he said.

items: 'Game changer' experimental drug doubles survival time for pancreatic cancer, trial shows

blocks.text: An ecosystem that forbids negotiation

Booth, who is also a health-services researcher at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., has been treating patients with pancreatic cancer — one of the most lethal forms of the disease — for more than 20 years.
He says U.S. drugs like daraxonrasib are approved and funded in an "ecosystem that essentially forbids" negotiation.
In Canada, Health Canada will give regulatory approval for doctors and hospitals to use a drug and then health authorities will work with the drug companies to determine a price.

items: A novel mRNA cancer vaccine helps cut the chances of melanoma tumor recurrence in major study

blocks.text: But in the U.S., he says, it's illegal for the government to negotiate with the pharmaceutical companies when they launch most new drugs — a rule that was eased slightly in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — allowing the manufacturers to set their own price.

The median net price for new drugs launched in the U.S. was more than $250,000 US last year, according to a new report from the Boston-based Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER), up more than 35 per cent from the $190,000 US median three years earlier.
California-based drug maker Revolution Medicines set its launch price for daraxonrasib at $480,000 US ($675,000 Cdn) annually, or $40,000 for a 30-day supply at wholesale cost.
Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada
Profits over patients

Booth recalls how he and many of his colleagues were "thrilled" to see a treatment like daraxonrasib, a pill targeting a specific mutation in pancreatic cancer cells, prove effective in clinical trials.

The research found daraxonrasib halted or reversed tumour progression in nearly a third of patients, compared with about 10 per cent of those given chemotherapy, and increased survival from less than seven months to roughly 13.
"It was a signal of hope that we finally started to see some progress in this very difficult disease," Booth told CBC News.
But the excitement faded when Revolution Medicines announced the price of the drug, marketed as Rasonque.
LISTEN | Is Canada too reliant on the global supply chain for pharmaceuticals:
Cost of Living9:13Why is Canada so vulnerable to drug shortages?
In a statement emailed to CBC News, Revolution Medicines said how much a patient pays out of pocket depends on factors including treatment duration and insurance coverage.
"Our goal is to establish a price that reflects meaningful therapeutic advancement while supporting patient access and continued scientific innovation," a spokesperson wrote.
But doctors whose patients may benefit from daraxonrasib question the price.
"Sometimes the prices they quote make absolutely no sense," said Dr. Ramy Saleh, an associate professor of oncology at McGill University who researches early-stage clinical trials.

"I'm not convinced as an oncologist or a researcher that when a drug is approved that it will cost half a million a year, he said. "I'm pretty sure to produce it is, you know, a fraction of that cost."

A Revolution Medicines facility in Redwood City, Calif. The company developed daraxonrasib, a new pancreatic cancer drug that has been approved in the U.S. but not yet in Canada. (Revolution Medicines)
Dr. Ralph Wong, a senior medical oncologist at CancerCare Manitoba, accuses the company of profiting off the backs of patients like his.
"I've had multiple patients in my practice crying because they can't access the drug," he said.

items: Ontario cancer patients speak out over disappointment with drug funding decision
What Trump's 'most favoured nation' drug pricing policy might mean for Canadians

blocks.text: Wong says it's "particularly galling" that Revolution Medicines set such a high benchmark price based on its clinical-trial results rather than what he considers a price that would support patient access.
He and other doctors say they do everything they can to get patients free access through clinical trials or compassionate-access programs.
But if a drug isn't approved by Health Canada or covered by public or private insurance, patients can be left to pay for it themselves.
Revolution Medicines has yet to apply for Canadian approval of daraxonrasib.
Drug doubles survival time for pancreatic cancer patients, trial shows
'Crippling' cost of longer life
While wealthy patients may be able to manage the price of a drug like daraxonrasib, Booth said it would be financially "crippling" for many.
Data from the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board (PMBRB), the arms-length federal agency that regulates patented drug prices, show Canadians are spending more on medications.

Sales of patented drugs reached $22.1 billion in 2024, up nearly 11 percent in a year, according to the PMPRB's most recent annual report. Patented medicines accounted for 47 per cent of all spending on medicines. There were 1,137 patented medicines approved for human use in Canada that year.

items: Why millions of Canadian taxpayer dollars are spent on U.S. medical treatments

blocks.text: And that doesn't include what some patients pay for medications that aren't available in Canada.
For Howard, paying for daraxonrasib is like making a "down payment for a condo every month" for the hope of prolonging his life.
"It's not sustainable long term," he said, especially with all of the hurdles involved in getting the drug, including crossing the border to pick up the prescription at a U.S. postal address.
"[But] if I can gain a quality of life which allows you to spend more time with family, that's a significant bonus for me."
Cancer costs Canadian patients $33K on average

articles.title: First Nations want tangible results as 'historic' first ministers' meeting opens
articles.summary: First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades, amid warnings and a planned protest against what the Assembly of…

image.caption: Assembly of First Nations chiefs and provincial premiers gather for a group photo at the AFN First Nations - First Ministers Meeting Day of Ceremony in Ottawa, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Keito Newman)

blocks.text: Indigenous·New

First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades, amid warnings and a planned protest against what the Assembly of First Nations is calling an "historic gathering."
Negotiations held all weekend to discuss potential outcomes, agreement
The warning 43 years ago was about good talk without action.

It's why Indigenous leaders approached prime minister Pierre Trudeau's 1983 first ministers conference on constitutional rights with caution — concerned about holding negotiations to hold more negotiations, and about skeptical premiers primed to listen but not understand.

On Monday, First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet again in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights, the first such meeting in two decades, with those same warnings looming over what the Assembly of First Nations is calling an "historic gathering."

"First Nations and Canada and the provinces are at a crossroads," Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) told CBC Indigenous. "Many chiefs have told us that they see this meeting as a chance to chart maybe a path forward, a new path forward."

At an AFN-organized ceremony on Sunday few would speculate on what the meeting's outcome will be, but for chiefs the mantra going in is "tangible results." They stressed it can't be a "one-and-done" event.

"We're a minority in our own country," said Kelsey Jacko, chief of Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta, "and everybody's living off the milk and honey of our lands, but we're being left out, so we need a seat at the table."
Indigenous leaders meet to amend the Canadian Constitution in 1982

AFN, a national advocacy organization, has circulated several discussion papers suggesting it might seek commitments on building economic prosperity, policing, constitutional rights, health and education.

Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty on Sunday declined to speculate on potential outcomes, saying the federal government's top priority is "to listen, to learn and to discuss how we can move forward."

The AFN also circulated among First Nations a draft of a "Declaration of a Shared Path Forward" to be considered at the meeting that, if agreed to, would commit the parties to continue these meetings on an annual basis.
"If this goes well, then maybe that's what's in the future," New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt told reporters walking into the ceremony on Sunday.

However Woodhouse Nepinak said Friday "you will not see a declaration" following the meeting because the AFN needs more time to consult its chiefs, with negotiations continuing on potential outcomes all weekend.
First such meeting since 2005
The last Indigenous-focused first ministers meeting was held in 2005 in Kelowna, B.C., seeking solutions to close the gap in living standards and yielding an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

To prepare for this meeting, Woodhouse Nepinak was thinking back to the 1983 Indigenous rights conference and its famous moments, beginning with Pierre Trudeau interrupting the chiefs' ceremonial opening prayer then answering it with prayer of his own, which she called "hard to watch."
Several premiers or their ministers attended the AFN's day of ceremony on Sunday. Prime Minister Mark Carney didn't attend but sent Alty in his place.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak at the AFN's Day of Ceremony on Sunday. (Brett Forester/CBC News)
The closed-door meeting comes as fundamental issues of Indigenous land title, self-determination and place in confederation remain fractious.
In Alberta last week, First Nations celebrated the decisive defeat of a separation referendum called by Premier Danielle Smith. Quebec just elected a new sovereigntist Parti Québécois government.
The B.C. Conservative Party, which campaigned on repealing the province's legislation on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, won a majority government on Saturday.
Federally, Carney proposed the meeting while facing backlash for his hyperfocus on fast-tracking development of major infrastructure and energy projects, pipelines in particular.
"Of course they want major projects," Woodhouse Nepinak reiterated,"but they're not going to get there without First Nations."

Speaking in French with Radio-Canada's Espaces autochtones, AFN's Quebec/Labrador Regional Chief Francis Verreault-Paul likened the situation facing First Nations to the one Canada faces, according to Carney, as a middle power on the world stage.
Verreault-Paul quoted Carney's headline-grabbing speech earlier this year in Davos, where he said,"if you are not at the table, you are on the menu."
“Right now, First Nations are not at the table for these major projects, " Verreault-Paul said.
Does that mean they're on the menu? Russ Diabo would probably say yes.
'Recipe for conflict'?
A member of the Mohawk Nation of Kahnawà:ke and a spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, Diabo helped organize a grassroots rally outside the meeting.
"We're challenging their mandate," he said, meaning AFN, "saying they don't have one to represent rights-holders, the inherent and treaty-rights holders."
AFN's national chief position is elected by chiefs and not popular vote among First Nations people. It also has no Alberta regional chief and sometimes faces questions about its relevance.
"It's a recipe for conflict, I think, because First Nations rights-holders weren't involved in this. It was just with chiefs — and select chiefs," Diabo said.

Three First Nations also raised those concerns in an open letter, warning about the meeting becoming "political cover" for the federal agenda. One signatory, Onion Lake Cree Nation on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border, also sent AFN a formal cease-and-desist notice.

"I'll be outside with the grassroots people," Onion Lake Chief Darwin Peter Chief said in an interview. "We're standing alongside First Nations in defence of our inherent treaty rights and independence and our right to determine our own future."

His community has serious and long-standing concerns about representation, transparency, meaningful consultation and the protection of treaty rights, he said, and wrote. Woodhouse Nepinak said she welcomes the peaceful protest.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.
With files from Radio-Canada's Dominique Degré

articles.title: Historic lawsuit challenging government over climate inaction begins trial hearings
articles.summary: After a seven year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.

image.caption: A fire this summer near Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. The youth applicants going to court this week are arguing that government inaction on climate change will violate their Charter rights. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science
After a seven year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.
Youth plaintiffs are arguing in Vancouver that climate inaction violates their Charter rights
After a seven-year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.

The lawsuit, launched by 15 youth applicants who claim their Charter rights to life, liberty and security of the person have been violated because of the government’s inadequate action on fighting climate change, was first filed in 2019. It was initially dismissed by the Federal Court, then sent back for a full hearing by the Federal Court of Appeal.

items: Ottawa argues youth-led climate change lawsuit too broad to be tried in court
Youth activists say Canada has legal duty to protect vital resources as public hearing ends

blocks.text: It is the most prominent of several legal challenges based on climate policy across Canada, and has gotten further than any others. This is the first time such a lawsuit will receive a full hearing in court, with the potential for a precedent-setting judgment that could influence Canadian law and inspire other climate lawsuits around the world.
Nine of the 15 youth plaintiffs in the case in Vancouver when it was first filed in 2019. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
What do the applicants want?
The applicants want the court to declare that not doing enough on climate action is, in fact, a violation of Canadians’ rights.

Their key argument is that the federal government’s landmark climate law, the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act, puts the country on an emissions trajectory that is inconsistent with a safe and livable future.

Essentially, the lawsuit argues that despite the government’s emissions targets and current policies to decarbonize, it still is not aligned with what scientists say is required to stave off the worst impacts of climate change.
“It's hard to see how our governments aren't taking the proper stand needed to combat this crisis because it seems so urgent to me,” said Sadie Vipond, one of the applicants in the case.

Vipond was seven years old when she remembers her grandmother waking her up in the middle of the night, telling her they needed to flee from rising waters during the 2013 Calgary floods. She was 13 when she joined the climate lawsuit, and has experienced many more climate-related disasters since then — wildfire smoke, extreme heat waves and a near-repeat of those Calgary floods. She’s now a student at the University of British Columbia studying environmental science.

As a remedy, Vipond and her fellow applicants want the government to develop a new climate plan that’s backed by the latest scientific evidence on avoiding climate impacts, and open to further judicial review to make sure it remains strong.
"I would like to see my country be able to take a stand for what I know is right," said Vipond.
How will the trial unfold?

The hearings begin on Monday, and the applicants and their expert witnesses will be testifying in the first two weeks. Vipond and other applicants will speak about the climate harms they have experienced — which have piled up in the past seven years as extreme heat, wildfires and flooding have touched the lives and millions of Canadians.

The applicants will have eight expert witnesses, including prominent climate scientists and experts in health, international law, clean energy and Indigenous rights. Two of their witnesses have been lead authors for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the premier global climate science agency that advises the UN.
The government is expected to present their side in the third week, with four witnesses who are experts in climate science, law and economics.

The government is not disputing that climate science is real and causing harm. But it is expected to argue that Canada's laws are not directly harming the youth plaintiffs, according to Columbia University's Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, which studies climate-related litigation worldwide.

A key legal debate in this case is whether Section 7 of the Charter, which guarantees life, liberty and security, imposes what's known as a "positive obligation" on the government. In other words: is the government constitutionally required to proactively protect Canadians from climate harms by enacting laws or other actions?

A court ruling on this question “would constitute a major development in Canadian constitutional law,” wrote human rights lawyer Catherine Savard, Canadian expert for the Sabin Center in New York City.
After the government witnesses, the hearings will take a break and both sides will return in February to make closing arguments.
The outcome will be closely watched around the world. The Canadian case is the first major climate trial since a landmark opinion from the International Court of Justice last year.

The global court found that countries could be in violation of international law if they didn’t take steps to reduce emissions, and countries that are suffering the impacts of climate disasters could seek compensation from the countries causing climate change.
“I think there is a very important role for the courts here in terms of protecting constitutional rights,” said David Wu, partner at the law firm Arvay Finlay who is representing the applicants.
“Are we going to allow governments to do what they want in terms of climate policy or targets or does our Constitution have something to say about it?”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: Montreal wants rent control, mandatory registry. What would that look like?
articles.summary: The city of Montreal passed a motion asking the Quebec government to create a mandatory rent registry and to cap rent increases to inflation over a three-year average. Housing advocates are praising…

image.caption: The city is asking the Quebec government to cap rent increases to inflation over a three-year average and to create a mandatory rent registry. (Ivanoh Demers/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

The city of Montreal passed a motion asking the Quebec government to create a mandatory rent registry and to cap rent increases to inflation over a three-year average. Housing advocates are praising the move, but not everyone is on board.
City says goal is to make rent increases more predictable, rental market more transparent
Nicolas Marion has been living in Montreal for the past 11 years, but now he's worried about being pushed out of his neighbourhood.
"I'm starting to reach the limit of what I can afford to pay," he told elected officials during a city council meeting on Monday.
Not only does Marion fear being pushed out, he's afraid of becoming homeless. He says renovations in his building aren't always necessary and are being used to generate profits.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada responded by saying his situation resonated with all those present, and that unfortunately it's a reality for many Montrealers who are struggling to keep up with rising rents.
"The work we are doing regarding homelessness isn't just about supporting those already living on the streets; it's also about turning off the tap to prevent others from ending up there," she said.
Marion shared his concerns shortly before council voted in favour of an amended motion on rent control and a mandatory rent registry.
Montreal adopts motion calling on Quebec to cap rent hikes, create mandatory rent registry

More specifically, the city is asking the Quebec government to cap rent increases to inflation over a three-year average to better control rent, with exceptions for major renovations and significant investment.
It's also asking the province to put in place a universal and accessible rent registry that would allow tenants to know the rent history of a property.
Projet Montréal's Elvira Carhuallanqui tabled the motion, saying the goal is "to make rent increases more predictable, and the rental market more transparent."
According to city officials, two thirds of Montreal households are renters.
Registry about restoring balance of information
Under Quebec law, landlords are supposed to disclose the lowest rent paid over a 12-month period, as stipulated by section G on the Quebec residential lease form.
Benoit Rullier, with the Coalition of Housing Committees and Tenants Associations of Quebec (RCLALQ), argues that section G is not effective when it comes to protecting tenants.

Vivre en Ville is a Quebec City non-profit organization dedicated to promoting sustainable communities. A recent study they carried out in collaboration with polling firm Leger indicates that 79 per cent of tenants in the province are either unaware whether their landlord had filled out section G of their lease, or knew that their landlord had not filled it out.
Without knowing what the previous rent was, it's difficult for tenants to prove a rent increase is unjustified or abusive.

items: Quebec has rent control. So why are apartment prices still soaring?

blocks.text: Rullier says a mandatory rent registry will allow for better enforcement of regulations.

David Wachsmuth, a professor of urban planning at McGill University, says that even with a rent registry, it would still be up to the tenant to make sure that the rent stays within the allowed limits.

"The key idea about a rental registry is to solve the problem of what economists would call 'information asymmetry,'" he said. The concept suggests that when one party has a lot more information than the other, it gives them negotiating advantages in a transaction.

"There's kind of one law that says, ‘Hey, here's the allowed rent increases,' but it doesn't amount to anything if both parties aren't in an equal position to verify that everybody's following the rules," he said.
What a rent registry could look like
Although it can be tricky to implement a new system with government oversight, Wachsmuth says there are a few options available.
He said the government could build on the framework of the registry implemented by Vivre en Ville, where current and past tenants can anonymously submit information about their rental units.
The data collected includes information such as street addresses, monthly rent price, rent adjustments and utility costs.

items: Quebec housing tribunal recommends a 3.1% basic rent increase
Montreal landlords under fire for rent increases as high as 20% in Park Ex

blocks.text: Another option, which would cost more and require more time and resources, would be for the province to require that leases be submitted into a government portal. Wachsmuth said the information could be verified, and then whatever is determined to be in the public interest could be posted.
Yet another possibility would be to piggyback off existing tax systems.

"Revenu Québec already has an enormous amount of apparatus to gather and verify everybody's income information, and so adding one additional hook into that system would make the rental market much more transparent," Wachsmuth said.
Rent registries have long been discussed in Quebec, but never implemented.
Quebec sees sharp rise in cost of homelessness services
Housing advocates and the City of Montreal hope that showing a united front will help nudge the new Parti Québécois government — which has said housing and homelessness are top priorities — to act.
Wachsmuth says, however, that as a minority government, the actions it might take will have a lot to do with the alliances it forms with other parties regarding housing policies.

items: The PQ won't be able to advance its agenda without cross-party support. Will anyone answer the call?

blocks.text: Rent control's merits debated by landlords
But not everyone supports the idea of a registry or rent control.

Éric Sansoucy, a spokesperson for Corporation des propriétaires immobiliers du Québec, a non-profit organization that represents and supports residential rental property owners and managers throughout Quebec, says the province already has enough safeguards in place.
Sansoucy pointed to a 2025 study by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) on rent-control laws which limit annual rent increases.

The study shows they can help current tenants with lower rents, but that there can be trade-offs, such as higher rents for vacant units. They can also lead to lower investments and repairs, the slowing down of new construction and reduced tenant mobility.

items: Quebec food banks facing historic demand, over 3 million service requests a month: report

blocks.text: Sansoucy says a registry would stifle maintenance without lowering market pressures, and favours a different approach to solving the housing crisis.
"The real solution is to help the people and provide direct financial assistance and housing allowances to low-income households," he said.
In the interim, the City of Montreal has agreed to continue funding for Vivre en Ville's registry, and to put some effort into making sure more tenants know the resource exists.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Annabelle Olivier is a digital journalist at CBC Montreal. She previously worked at Global News as an online producer. You can reach her at anne.isabelle.olivier@cbc.ca.
With files from Gabriel Guindi

articles.title: NBI files cyberlibel, obstruction of justice referral vs. ex-Sara Duterte aide Jefry Tupas
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Monday filed a referral with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 3:59pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Monday filed a referral with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas.
The complaint was for cyberlibel, obstruction of justice, and publication of false news.

“We will be filing… a case of obstruction of justice, cyberlibel, and publication of false news under the Revised Penal Code will be filed against Jefry Tupas,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said in a press briefing.
“So we’re endorsing it to the DOJ for proper disposition,” he added.
This stemmed from the sworn statement submitted by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Gracioso claimed that he delivered cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao Representative Paolo Duterte on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
He also claimed that Tupas received the cash on behalf of the Vice President.
Tupas has denied Gracioso’s claims and submitted his affidavit with the bureau. He alleged that NBI agents offered him cash and a place to stay in the upscale Forbes Park in Makati City.
The Tupas camp has yet to issue a statement.
Similarly, Sara Duterte, Paolo Duterte, and Velasco have submitted affidavits denying the allegations against them.
Paolo Duterte has also filed a cyberlibel complaint against Matibag, Gracioso as well as GMA Network executives and journalists. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: House leaders defend 2027 budget amendments amid questions over project details
articles.summary: House leaders on Monday defended the amendments made by the chamber to the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, saying these were purportedly based on agency proposals and had been made…

blocks.text: House leaders on Monday defended the amendments made by the chamber to the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, saying these were purportedly based on agency proposals and had been made on valid grounds.

House appropriations panel Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia of Bataan and Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno of Antipolo made the statements amid criticisms from civil society organizations and opposition lawmakers over projects allegedly bearing questionable documentation and incorrect coordinates.

“These [amendments made by House members] are validated projects from the agency. You cannot make amendments in the GAB (General Appropriations Bill) with a project that is not validated by the DA (Department of Agriculture), DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) and so forth,” Garcia said at a press conference.

Garcia urged critics to identify the projects with questionable coordinates, saying these could be checked and corrected if necessary. He said the cited errors might have resulted from typographical mistakes in the voluminous budget documents.

“Context changes everything. Kung may mga nakikitang mga projects na mali, 'yung mga coordinates, maganda ma-identify natin para ma-check natin. At kung kailangan i-rectify, i-rectify ho natin. Maaaring nagkaroon ng typographical error because of the voluminous documents," he said.
(If there are erroneous entries, we ask them to identify the projects involved so we can correct them. These could also be typographical errors.)

"Maybe if the People's Budget Coalition can be more specific with the projects involved, so we can validate them. Because if we don’t have the list of these projects, we cannot validate them,” Garcia added.
Asked whether he meant that the House had nothing to do with the incorrect coordinates, Garcia replied, “Of course.”

“In our case, these farm-to-market roads, including those in our amendments, were validated by provincial agriculturists, municipal agriculturists and the regional office of the DA. These are validated roads,” Garcia added.

Garcia was reacting to pronouncements by the People’s Budget Coalition, which questioned the inclusion of thousands of infrastructure projects in the House-approved budget, saying many lacked publicly available supporting documents, including programs of work and certifications of implementability.

The group also flagged farm-to-market road projects whose coordinates reportedly pointed to bodies of water, as well as concerns over project costs and the alignment of some projects with infrastructure master plans.
In a separate finding, the coalition said the House added billions of pesos for multipurpose buildings and local access roads while reducing funding for foreign-assisted infrastructure projects.
No lump-sum allocations
Puno, meanwhile, said lawmakers based their amendments on agency proposals and consultations with their constituents, adding that Congress reviews rather than originates the national budget.

“People should know that Congress does not create the budget. Agencies submit their budget to us, and we're just reviewing what has already been submitted to us. If there is an error, we’ll correct it. [This means] if they give us a lump-sum amount and they don't give us individual details on that, of course, we are going to flag it,” Puno said.
He clarified that lawmakers could not insert projects into the budget supposedly without the concerned agency’s clearance.

“If we can give the details [of the project], of course, we will give it. And when the appropriations committee ‘inserts’ things there, they cannot do it without the clearance of the agency because there is even an additional safeguard that is created by the agencies, particularly public works," Puno said.
"All of those requirements will be submitted to them prior to implementation,” he added.
Puno said the safeguards required before a project can be approved include:

items: Accurate project coordinates
Approval from the regional development council
Consent from the local government, among other requirements

blocks.text: “What are we worried about? I do not agree with everything that is in that budget, but I respect the people who did it. We will give them the proper recognition for whatever work they put into it and whatever mistakes they have committed, the Senate can correct,” Puno said.
“But you cannot throw in blanket accusations that really speak to nothing,” he added.
Puno said the DPWH's proposed 2027 budget, as submitted to the House, contained lump-sum allocations. He said the House addressed this by specifying the intended purposes of the funds.

“Congress had to fill up the blanks because what was submitted to us were lump sums, and this was balanced out by the DPWH issuing certain regulations and requirements that prevented the arbitrary inclusion of the projects,” Puno said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.

blocks.text: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This years plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past Plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This Plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.summary: Motorists will see mixed fuel price changes starting October 27.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 3:18pm

Early travelers start arriving at bus terminals in Cubao, Quezon City on Monday to secure tickets and beat the possible surge of passengers heading to different provinces to pay their respect to departed loved ones for All Soul's Day.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Mixed fuel price adjustments will take effect Tuesday, October 27, with diesel and kerosene becoming more expensive while gasoline prices decline.
The Department of Energy announced the following changes Monday:

items: Diesel — up P1.20 per liter
Gasoline — down P0.30 per liter
Kerosene — up P0.50 per liter

blocks.text: The adjustments will remain in effect until Monday, November 2.
Last week, diesel prices rose by P2.60 per liter, while gasoline and kerosene prices fell by P4.30 and P1 per liter, respectively.
Industry forecasts late last week had pointed to larger adjustments for both diesel and gasoline.
Global supply pressures
The DOE said this week's price movements were mainly influenced by global oil prices amid supply pressures linked to conflict in the Middle East.
At the Singapore International Energy Week, Saudi Arabia announced an arrangement to store crude oil at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns beginning in mid-2027.

"This arrangement enhances the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia, as well as contributes to Singapore's energy security and resilience in the event of supply disruptions," Singapore Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said.

Saudi Arabia's Minister of Energy and Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman Al Saud also reaffirmed the kingdom's commitment to maintaining reliable energy supplies despite tensions in the region.
"Bringing supply closer to key Asian markets would strengthen the flexibility of our supply network and support Singapore's security of supply and preparedness," Al Saud said in a video recording.
The Singapore International Energy Week runs from October 26 to 30.

articles.title: 'Modus'?: Ombudsman urges DOJ probe into Philip Lustre arrest process
articles.summary: Lustre's lawyer said the journalist never received a subpoena or notice before his arrest.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 3:03pm

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called on the Department of Justice (DOJ) to investigate the circumstances that led to veteran journalist Philip Lustre's arrest after his lawyer said he never received a subpoena or notice about the cyberlibel complaint against him.

In an interview with reporters on Monday, October 26, Remulla, a former justice secretary, pointed to a known "modus" in which complainants deliberately provide prosecutors with the wrong address of a respondent.

"Ano iyan, may modus kasi iyan. 'Yung mga nagfa-file ng kaso, binibigyan ng wrong address ang prosecutor," Remulla said after the signing of a memorandum of understanding with the Justice Sector Coordinating Council at the Supreme Court.
("There's a modus there. Those filing cases give prosecutors the wrong address.")
"Kailangan diyan maimbestigahan ng DOJ 'yan. Kung ano nangyari kasi nga bakit hindi dumating? Ano nangyari sa subpoena? Ano nangyari sa documents na pinadala sa respondent-accused?" he added.
("The DOJ needs to investigate what happened. Why didn't it arrive? What happened to the subpoena? What happened to the documents sent to the respondent-accused?")
Remulla said prosecutors should not merely rely on information provided by complainants and have a duty to exercise due diligence.
"It should not happen," Remulla said, referring to the circumstances raised in Lustre's case.
Arrested over cyber libel. Lustre, a veteran journalist, was arrested while attending a news forum in Quezon City on Saturday, October 24.
He was arrested on the strength of a warrant issued by the Regional Trial Court Branch 10 in Davao City in connection with a cyber libel case.
According to Lustre's lawyer, Dino de Leon, the journalist was unaware of the complaint before his arrest.
De Leon said Lustre had not received a subpoena or notice that would have given him an opportunity to answer the complaint during the preliminary investigation.

articles.title: [New Rx] The Philippines is getting older. What if we treated experience as an asset?
articles.summary: Rather than treating retirement as the expiration of professional value, the Philippines should create markets to harness the accumulated expertise and judgment of older workers as a productive…

blocks.text: The Philippines still thinks of itself as a young country. For decades, our demographic advantage has meant millions of young workers entering the labor force, staffing BPO offices, hospitals, factories and businesses here and abroad.
That advantage will not last forever.

According to the 2024 Census of Population from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 11.42 million Filipinos were already aged 60 or older in 2024, representing 10.2% of the household population. In 2020, the share was only 8.5%. PSA population projections suggest that by 2055, people aged 60 and above could account for about 19.6% of the population. PSA population projections
Almost every discussion of this transition begins with the costs.
More pensions. More chronic diseases. More hospital care. Greater demand for long-term care. Fewer working-age people supporting more retirees.
Those concerns are real. But they also encourage us to think about older people mainly as liabilities on the national balance sheet.
What if we looked at the other side?
A Filipino does not wake up on his 60th birthday having suddenly lost 35 years of accumulated knowledge, professional relationships and judgment.

Consider a 63-year-old physician. She may no longer want hospital nights, a full clinic or a 60-hour workweek. But she could spend 10 hours a week reviewing clinical cases for an international research organization. She could evaluate medical charts, mentor younger physicians, advise a biotechnology company, review drug-safety reports or teach clinical reasoning.

A retired nurse could train virtual-care teams. A former pharmaceutical executive could advise several startups. A retired banker could sit on investment committees. A former regulator could guide companies through systems that took him decades to understand.
What these people possess is difficult to manufacture quickly: judgment, networks, institutional memory, pattern recognition and credibility.
These are not simply social assets. They have economic value.
Some countries have already recognized pieces of this problem.

In Singapore, the government raised the statutory retirement age to 64 and the re-employment age to 69 from July 2026. Eligible employees must be offered re-employment, while programs such as the Senior Employment Credit subsidize employers who retain older workers. Singapore has explicitly described the objective as allowing seniors to remain productive while helping employers retain experienced workers. Singapore Ministry of Manpower on senior re-employment

Japan has gone further in encouraging continued employment. Its latest policy framework sets targets to raise employment among people aged 60 to 69 and expand measures allowing people to work until 70. It also supports job matching through public employment services and the country’s long-established Silver Human Resources Centers. Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare policy on older workers
These are important models.
But they still largely approach aging through the lens of employment longevity: how to keep older people in work, improve retirement adequacy and reduce the economic pressures of an aging society.
There is a further step the Philippines could explore.
Instead of simply asking how older workers can stay employed longer, ask how their accumulated expertise can be organized, matched with demand, digitized and sold as an economic service.
In other words, treat experience itself as a productive national asset.
Technology now makes that increasingly possible.
A person does not have to choose between a 50-hour workweek and complete retirement. Someone could work five hours a week. Ten hours. One project every quarter. One board meeting a month.

A retired specialist in Manila could review clinical data from the United States. A former executive in Cebu could advise a Singapore company remotely. A Filipino professional who spent 30 years overseas could mentor local entrepreneurs without permanently relocating home.
The objective should not be to force older Filipinos to work longer.

People who have worked for decades deserve pensions, healthcare and the freedom to stop working. Some will have health conditions that make continued employment difficult. Others will simply want retirement.
The goal is productive choice.
Those who remain healthy, capable and interested should not discover that the economy has no use for them unless they return to a conventional full-time job.

The World Health Organization itself cautions against equating aging with loss of productivity or contribution. WHO notes that older people contribute through paid and unpaid work, caregiving, communities and the transfer of knowledge, and argues that spending that enables their participation should be considered an investment rather than simply a cost. WHO on ageing, productivity and contribution
Artificial intelligence may make this opportunity even more important.
AI can summarize a medical chart. But an experienced physician may recognize that it missed the one detail that changes the diagnosis.
AI can generate a regulatory document. Someone who has dealt with regulators for 30 years may know which apparently minor sentence will create problems later.
AI can produce a financial model. An executive who has lived through several crises may recognize assumptions that look mathematically correct but make no commercial sense.
As machines become better at routine work, human judgment may become more valuable, not less.
Healthcare offers an obvious opportunity for the Philippines to test this idea.

The Philippines already had an estimated $4.2-billion healthcare-services outsourcing industry employing around 190,000 people in 2024, according to government industry-promotion materials. Its activities already include clinical support, medical coding, chart abstraction, data management and clinical-trial monitoring. CITEM’s Healthcare Philippines industry report

At the same time, the broader Philippine IT-BPM industry now employs about 1.9 million workers and generates more than $40 billion in annual revenue. IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines

The next evolution of healthcare outsourcing could require less repetitive processing and more clinical judgment, pharmacovigilance, research support, medical review, regulatory affairs, real-world evidence and AI supervision.
That creates an unusual opportunity for older professionals.
A global pharmaceutical company may value a Filipino physician with 30 years of oncology experience for five hours a week more than another full-time junior processor.
A startup may not be able to hire a former hospital CEO, but it could afford her expertise several hours a month.
A young physician entering clinical research may gain enormously from someone who has spent decades navigating hospitals, ethics boards, regulators and professional societies.

Imagine a national marketplace through which Philippine and foreign companies could find retired or semi-retired Filipino doctors, scientists, engineers, accountants, bankers, teachers and executives for fractional assignments.

Professional societies could maintain expert networks. Universities could create senior-fellow pools. BPO companies could develop global expertise-as-a-service businesses. Retired Filipinos abroad could participate remotely.
Instead of exporting only Filipino labor, the Philippines could increasingly export Filipino judgment.

The benefits would extend beyond another paycheck. Older people could maintain income and engagement if they want it. Younger workers gain mentors. SMEs gain access to expertise they could never afford full time. Professional networks are transferred rather than disappearing. Decades of accumulated human capital remain inside the productive economy.
The traditional demographic equation is simple:
More older Filipinos = more healthcare + more pensions + greater dependency.
That equation is incomplete.
There is another side:
More experienced Filipinos = more knowledge + networks + mentorship + productive capacity.
Both are true.

Countries such as Singapore and Japan have institutionalized important parts of senior employment. The Philippines can learn from them, but it can also go further: not simply extending working lives, but deliberately creating markets for what older people know.
That distinction matters because the Philippines is likely to age while it is still trying to become a much wealthier country.

We cannot afford an economy in which millions of people spend four decades accumulating expertise and then, because they cross an arbitrary age threshold, most of that economic capital becomes invisible.
The challenge is not to make Filipinos work forever.
It is to stop treating experience as something that expires at retirement.
An aging population will cost the Philippines money.
The more interesting question is how much value the country is allowing to retire with it. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

articles.title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
articles.summary:
Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little…
articles.byline: Julian Borger, Sufian Taha and Quique Kierszenbaum in Hebron

blocks.text: Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.

A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.

Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.

As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.

The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro, who was forced to flee his home in the Deir Baha area of Hebron by Israeli security forces, looks at his house from a distance.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.

“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro’s house in Hebron, now a military position, with netting over its upper floors Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.

The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.

“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”

By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.

“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.

blocks.caption: Wasam Sadi, a Palestinian driver, has difficulties with his vision after he was attacked in his truck by Israeli settlers near the entrance of Hebron.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.

“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.
Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by floodwaters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.
Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday.
They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident around 11.15am.
There were no reports of physical injuries, Queensland Police said in a statement.
Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.
There are warnings of more rain and flooding to come.
Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.
The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.
Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.
Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.
Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.
On Sunday evening, thunderstorms were briefly connected from southern Queensland to Bass Strait, as a swift-moving system passed towards Australia’s east coast.
The storm band raced over most states, propelled by strong winds in the upper atmosphere.
“But that steering wind sort of just tapered off through the night last night over [Queensland’s] Darling Downs,” Hines said.
Flood warnings are current for Warrill Creek and the Bremer River in the Lockyer Valley, the Macintyre and Moonie rivers in the south, and the Mary River near the Sunshine Coast.
Western Queensland also remains on alert, with warnings current for the Warrego River at Charleville, the Bulloo River in Quilpie, and the Barcoo River at Blackall.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.
Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

articles.title: [EDITORIAL] Post-Lustre arrest: Decriminalize libel and cyber libel
articles.summary: Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy

blocks.text: Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy
Nitong Sabado, inaresto si Philip Lustre Jr., isang beteranong mamamahayag at may akda ng Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines.

Diin sa salitang Sabado — dahil palatandaan ito ng harassment — lalo na kung ang pag-aresto ay nakatali sa malayong korte tulad ng Davao City. Halimbawa, kung inaresto ka ng gabi ng Biyernes, Sabado, o Linggo, kahit pa may naka-duty na judge sa isang night court, malaki ang probability na ilang gabi kang matutulog sa kulungan, lalo na kung hahagilapin o ire-request mo pa sa ibang ahensiya o barangay ang required papers.
Maraming red flag na weaponization ng batas ang pag-aresto kay Lustre.
First red flag: Ginamit ang paboritong batas ng mga bully: ang cyber libel law. Ito rin ang ginamit laban kay Maria Ressa at Reynaldo Santos ng Rappler.

Nito lang nakaraang linggo, nag-file ng cyber libel complaint ang kapatid ni Bise Presidente Sara Duterte, si Davao Congressman Paolo Duterte, laban sa mga opisyal, staff, at reporter ng GMA 7. Inihain ang complaint dahil sa istoryang inilabas ng network tungkol sa graft case ng magkapatid na may kinalaman sa whistleblower na si Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Second red flag: Secret warrant. Walang notification ng complaint mula sa prosecutor, at lightning arrest ang nangyari. Under normal procedure, inaabisuhan ang aarestuhin, at may right of reply ang subject ng complaint.
Third red flag: Unknown case filed by an unknown complainant. Ang tanging alam ng kampo ni Lustre ay ang korte at hukom na naglabas ng arrest warrant — si Davao City Judge Retrina Fuentes.

Si Fuentes ang siya ring judge na naglabas ng warrant noong 2022 laban kay Walden Bello, isang academic at dating congressman, dahil sa umano’y cyber libel na nagmula sa reklamo ni Jefry Tupas, long time aide ng Bise Presidente.
Classic intimidation tactic ito ng media — kahit bailable ang kaso mo, ipatitikim ng complainant sa ’yo ang pait na makulong kahit isang gabi lang.

Kapag nasisilayan ng liwanag ng investigative journalism ang korupsiyon at pang-aabuso ng kapangyarihan, madalas ginagamit ang batas na punyal ng personal na vendetta, imbes na kalasag para sa pangangalaga ng publiko.
Desperado ba ang mga Duterte na agawin ang naratibo lalo ngayong tila hindi pumapabor sa Bise Presidente ang daloy ng paglilitis sa impeachment trial niya?
Nagshi-shift na ba ang mga anak ni Rodrigo Duterte mula sa victimhood narrative sa paborito ng ama nilang fear tactics?
Matagal nang panawagan ng Rappler ang decriminalization of libel.
Noong 2012, nanindigan ang Rappler na ang criminalized libel at cyber libel ay banta sa free speech at press freedom. Lalo nang pinatunayan ‘yan ng kasaysayan.
Decriminalize libel and cyberlibel. Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy.
Habang pinapayagan ng batas na ikulong ng estado at ng makapangyarihang mga pulitiko ang mga mamamahayag — laging nanganganib ang press freedom sa Pilipinas.

Mula sa drug war killings ni Rodrigo Duterte, ang mga mansion ni dating speaker Martin Romualdez sa ibang bansa, hanggang sa pandarambong ng elected officials sa flood control corruption — lahat ‘yan ay nabunyag sa pamamagitan ng media.
Let media continue shining the light. Decriminalize libel and cyber libel. – Rappler.com
