articles.title: Brazil keeps left: what Lula’s victory means for his country and beyond
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured victory in the presidential race, we look the implications for democracy, the environment and international relations

Good…

blocks.text: Good morning. Chances are you woke this morning to news of two momentous election results. In Serbia, a student-led movement has ousted the country’s long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić (which you can read more about here). And just hours ago, Brazil’s president staged a sensational turnaround against his far-right opponent after a nail-biting vote.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, won a forth nonconsecutive term as president, seeing off far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who spearheaded the radical populist movement built by his father and former president, Jair. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.

After Bolsonaro’s surprise first-round victory earlier this month, the Workers’ party incumbent Lula pulled off a historic fightback – a consolidation of the democratic resurgence the country has enjoyed since he took office – and an early birthday present for the veteran leftist, who turns 81 on Tuesday.

But with Bolsonaro refusing to accept the result, the victory is a tense one. I spoke to the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips, who was in São Paulo at the Workers’ party vote count, to find out what the result means and what may lie ahead.
Weekend roundup

items: UK news | Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.
Crime | British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

France | Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

UK politics | Prime minister Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
Aviation | Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘This is the crescendo of Lula’s incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career’

blocks.caption: This morning’s results were an unprecedented turnaround, according to election analysts. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: When the results were declared just after midnight UK time, the choice of Brazil’s 159 million voters was narrow, but clear. The 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote to his rival’s 48.21% – about 4.3m votes – in what Lula called “a defeat for denialism”.
A visibly angry Bolsonaro has already refused to concede, citing a decision to extend voting for an extra two hours – although both sides had called for it, for different reasons.
The outcome was an unprecedented turnaround after a populist surge in first-round voting at the beginning of the month left Brazil’s progressives reeling.

In those early October elections, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – putting the 45-year-old scion of the authoritarian clan in pole position: not once, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
In the intervening weeks, the polls tightened dramatically, putting Bolsonaro ahead by only fractions of a percentage point.

“This is the crescendo of an incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career,” Tom says. I can hear crowds of Lula supporters cheering in the background as we speak, and fireworks exploding. “It saw Lula go from rural poverty to union leader to the first elected working-class leader of Brazil, who has helped millions of people escape poverty and rode a commodities boom in his first two terms”.

For Brazil, a Lula win represents stability and the assurance that the country’s democratic future is secure, at least in the short term. “Over the past four years, Lula has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by more than 70%. He’s come to the help of the Indigenous people who live there. He’s cracked down on illegal mining,” Tom tells me. “It’s very positive news is that all this will continue.”
How did Lula turn things around?

“Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo, told Tom earlier this month, pointing to a series of societal shifts have contributed to this.
Evangelical Christianity has expanded across Brazil in recent decades, with church leaders throwing their support behind the socially conservative policies favoured by Bolsanaro Sr and Jr.

Pro-gun Flavio Bolsonaro harnessed voter frustration at chronic levels of urban crime and violence. Despite being embedded in Brazilian politics for decades, he successfully portrayed himself as an anti-establishment outsider, using social media far more effectively than his rival.

And others believe he had significant help: a dozen watchdogs and research groups have published reports alleging that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign. The controversy grew after Brazils’ electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”, while the company called the allegations “false and unfounded”.

Progressives were galvanised after the first-round results revealed a record abstention rate of 21%, more common among Lula-supporting groups such as lower-income voters, and their focus sharpened on mobilisation. Millions joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s army”, which sent out daily instructions on how to make supportive content go viral. The 80-year-old incumbent, who only took ownership of his first smartphone in recent days, started posting to Instagram and TikTok. For the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook that of Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign was hit by a succession of scandals. In a revelation that made the UK’s partygate seem tame by comparison, last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of the 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party along with sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to cut deals with his father’s government.

Amid speculation that a comeback might be possible, at a million-strong rally on Copacabana beach in Rio on Saturday, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “We are going to turn this around!”
And so he did.
What role did Trump play in the election?

The US president has boasted about “lots of people that I got elected” in Latin America, styling himself as a kingmaker after a succession of right-wing candidates aligned with Washington have won power.

Although Donald Trump did not openly endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, his influence loomed large. Last year, he denounced the supreme court trial of his ally Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch-hunt”, imposing extraordinary 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports as retribution for what he claimed was political persecution.

Lula has styled himself as the country’s defender against Trump’s “colonial” designs. His victory consolidates a multilateral foreign policy and pragmatic approach to relations with the US, China and Russia. He has rejected invitations to join the controversial coalition of Latin American countries conducting military operations against drug cartels alongside the Pentagon, which would have resulted in much greater US involvement on Brazilian soil.

Furthermore, a win for pro-democracy campaigners in one country may serve to bolster international counterparts. As our senior international correspondent Julian Borger sets out in this compelling piece, along with the Brazil vote, a series of high-stakes elections in Serbia yesterday, Israel on Tuesday and the US next week are closely interlinked, and Lula’s win may have global ramifications, as leaders across Latin America and the world congratulate him this morning.
What does the result mean for the environment, in Brazil and beyond?

Last week, Tom travelled to Roraima, the northern state where Bolsonaro registered his best result nationwide. On his trip, he heard first-hand from Indigenous leaders and conservationists on why the populist’s success was causing panic.

His father’s environmentally devastating administration facilitated an illegal gold rush – turbo-charged by record global gold prices – that ravaged the Yanomami Indigenous reserve on the northern reaches of the Amazon.

When Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, the left-winger launched an environmentalist mission to expel the illegal miners, taking on the multibillion dollar extraction industry. Alongside wider green policies, he reduced deforestation in the Amazon to record lows.
“Tragically,” says Tom, “the environment only came up in the final presidential debate of this campaign.”

“Given that the Amazon makes up such a large portion of Brazil, and how important that region is to the global climate crisis, it’s amazing that it’s not been debated more. But people were voting more on economy, public security and culture war issues.”
In that final debate last Friday, Tom says that Lula “tried to show off the excellent, if incomplete, work that his government’s done in protecting the environment”.
Many will be relieved at Bolsonaro’s loss, as his vision for the Amazon was almost identical to his father’s.

While a Lula victory brings hope that these policies will continue, he will be working with a newly elected congress that features a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
How will Bolsonaro respond?
after newsletter promotion
The immediate aftermath of the election results is likely to be fraught, warns Tom, with Flávio Bolsonaro saying it was “impossible to concede the election result”.

“The Bolsonaro response is exactly as I feared but I don’t think it will mean very much,” Tom says. “All these world leaders are now recognising Lula’s win and I don’t think Bolsonaro has a hope of overturning this result”.

Tom suspects that in the coming days Bolsonaro will head to the States, to avoid ongoing criminal investigations. “That’s not to say there might not be violence from his supporters, but his political career is done. The fact they’ve lost is a sign that the name ‘Bolsonaro’ is toxic for a slight majority of Brazilian people.”
The week to come

items: Tuesday | Israel goes to the polls on Tuesday, amid orders from prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank after recent checkpoint attacks. His government will be fighting for its survival.

Wednesday | On Wednesday Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first budget statement in the House of Commons, which is expected to give local authorities more spending powers, as a means to promote growth

Thursday and Friday | European and Canadian leaders will meet in Montreal for the 21st EU-Canada summit, to discuss security and strategic cooperation. It will be the first opportunity for leaders to iron out details over a proposed invitation for Canada to become the EU’s first ever “associate member”

blocks.text: What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: Actor and producer Greg Wise. Photograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The Guardian

items: Greg Wise is bracingly open about his experience of IVF and how his struggle to conceive with his wife, fellow actor Emma Thompson, left him questioning his masculinity. Klara Kubiak, newsletters team
I enjoyed Ioan Marc Jones this morning, on how bell hooks revolutionised his worldview and got him to start telling the men in his life he loves them. Poppy Noor, acting head of newsletters
As someone who isn’t the biggest fan of feet, I found Chloe Mac Donnell’s piece about the current trend for ugly footwear equal parts fascinating and horrifying. Klara

I found Emma Beddington’s advice to teens wanting to know about the world of work – which includes the values of a pack of biscuits and realising that your boss sometimes just might be an idiot – in equal parts funny and wise. Poppy

blocks.text: Sport

blocks.caption: Michael Carrick said ‘it’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it’ after Manchester United’s defeat by Bournemouth. Photograph: Gary Oakley/EPA

blocks.text: Football | Manchester United’s hierarchy are in crisis talks over whether or not to sack Michael Carrick as head coach after he oversaw another torrid defeat, against Bournemouth at Old ­Trafford on Sunday, that left his job in the balance.
Formula One | The 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli won from Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen and should become F1’s youngest world champion next week in Mexico
Cricket | Shadab Khan made an unbeaten 113 in a thrilling last-wicket stand with Haris Rauf as Pakistan, chasing 242, beat England in a thriller
The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “‘Red Wall’ MPs wary as Burnham calls for EU free movement debate”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while Metro writes “Get Brexit Redone”.

The i Paper has “Streeting vows UK will ‘lead from the front’ as billions planned for defence boost”, the Times writes “Budget set to offer tax reprieve for pensioners” while the Express says “PM’s betrayal may ‘open door’ to EU migrants”.

Elsewhere, the Telegraph has “BBC’s £400k payout over anti-Semitism” and the FT has “Luxury houses shed €250bn in value as China’s shoppers tighten their belts”. The Mirror leads on “Meghan Dad ‘net will widen’” and the Mail has “Markle ‘abuser of worst kind’”.
Today in Focus

blocks.caption: Who ultimately has benefited from the UAE’s investment in Manchester?  Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Getty

blocks.text: How Abu Dhabi bought Andy Burnham’s Manchester
Today in Focus presenter and city resident Helen Pidd walks through modern Manchester – where Burnham was mayor for nearly a decade – and charts its transformation wrought by Emirati money.

Helen talks to North of England editor Josh Halliday too about how Abu Dhabi came to Manchester, alleged “sweetheart deals” it struck to own so much land, and a lack of transparency about it all even now.
Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld

blocks.caption: Illustration: Tom Gauld/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Cory’s shearwater fledglings on Corvo Island in the Azores.  Photograph: Andrea Zanenga

blocks.text: Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling seabirds fly to the ocean guided by the stars.

Since 2019, the 450 or so inhabitants of the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago have switched off the lights for five nights to tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters. The campaign started after the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters, who spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean. Many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing on the streets of the island’s only village, Vila do Corvo. By going dark, the stars can be seen clearly, allowing the juvenile birds safe passage to the ocean.

articles.title: Angus Taylor criticised for ‘tone deaf’ response to alleged attack on Helen Haines
articles.summary:
Zali Steggall and Monique Ryan say Coalition leader was wrong to deny link between parliamentary debate and political violence

Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to

blocks.text: Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to the alleged attack on Helen Haines, with crossbenchers Monique Ryan and Zali Steggall labelling a speech by the opposition leader “tone deaf” and saying he did not “read the room”.

Parliament returned in Canberra on Monday, a week after an alleged attack outside the Indi MP’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs. A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated.
The episode has sparked debate about the safety of MPs and the state of the political environment, including the culture of parliamentary debates.
But the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce have rejected calls for a change in practice to cool Australia’s political debate.
“In the past week, it has been suggested by some there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence,” Taylor said. “I disagree with this view.
“The Westminster system is about settling differences through robust and rigorous debate, not violence.

“Importantly, we debate with adversarial vigour, but we never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence. People who resort to intimidation and violence cross a line that must never be crossed.”

He said Labor had been correct to call out far-right extremism in Australia but called for all extremism to be rejected. He said judges should “come down harder” on people found guilty of intimidation or violence.
“Another thing we must do is celebrate Australia more readily. Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history.
“Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?”
Joyce told News24 his thoughts and prayers remained with Haines and her family, calling the alleged attack “so unAustralian”.

“Unfortunately what we’re seeing in Australia and around the world is a change in dynamics,” Joyce said. “I think parliament has got its part to play but I don’t think it’s going to be a solution to the problem.
“The issues, such as the Palestinian march across the [Sydney Harbour] Bridge, the vindictive, arsenic type of rhetoric that we see in the public realm, these are all part of it.
“I think it’s foolish to think if question time changes, Australia changes. Not necessarily, in fact highly unlikely.”
Steggall, the independent Warringah MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said she was personally disappointed by Taylor’s speech.
“There is a link between our words and actions,” she said.
“I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn.

“To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, make sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of parliament.”
She said the same caution should be applied to media reporting, election advertising and social media posts.
Steggall referenced conversations with Haines’ husband, Phil Haines, in Canberra on Monday.
“His words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate,” she said.
“We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.”
Ryan, the Kooyong independent, called Taylor’s response “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”.
“If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party,” she told ABC TV.
“If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.”

articles.title: House increases DPWH budget for Sandro Marcos’ district by P4.3B – watchdog
articles.summary: The People's Budget Coalition flags nearly 7,000 DPWH projects worth P190 billion without published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget

blocks.text: KEY POST. Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos leads the floor after being elected House majority leader on July 28, 2025.
Sandro Marcos' Facebook
The People's Budget Coalition flags nearly 7,000 DPWH projects worth P190 billion without published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget

items: Ilocos Norte's 1st District received the largest increase in public works funding, with an allocation of P4.74 billion in the House-approved budget for 2027, up from P369 million in the original proposal.

Concerns were raised during a Senate hearing regarding nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion added by the House without published documentation, prompting calls for the Senate to veto these additions.

Other districts represented by top House officials also saw significant budget increases, with the second and third largest hikes going to Davao de Oro's 2nd District and Misamis Occidental's 2nd District.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The congressional district of House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos in Ilocos Norte received the biggest increase in public works funding in the approved House spending bill for 2027, according to a budget watchdog.

Based on the transparency portal of volunteer-driven civic technology movement BetterGov.ph, Ilocos Norte’s 1st District was allocated P4.74 billion in project lists from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in the House version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
This is a significant increase of P4.38 billion from the P369 million that was originally proposed for the district in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

The NEP is also called the President’s budget, a proposal submitted annually by the executive to Congress. The House, which is constitutionally mandated to come up with an appropriations bill, may amend that proposal.
BetterGov.ph said its portal does not make allegations of irregularity or wrongdoing by a public official, and only compares changes between the NEP and the House GAB.

“The (district engineering office) mapping associates offices with legislative districts; it does not establish that a representative requested, sponsored, or controlled a project, or that each project lies in every district associated with its office,” the website disclaimer reads.
During a Senate hearing though on Monday, October 26, Ken Abante of People’s Budget Coalition flagged the increases.

“Nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion were inserted by the House without published project attachments,” Abante said, adding that many of these projects involve the construction of multi-purpose buildings.

“If there are no published documents, the Senate should remove them. The Senate should veto them,” he added. “Our concern is that the House has still not learned its lesson or felt any shame, despite our marches and rallies.”
Rappler has asked Marcos’ office why and how the House decided to increase public works funding for his district by billions of pesos. We will update this story once his office replies.

Second and third on the list are the DPWH offices in Davao de Oro’s 2nd District and Misamis Occidental’s 2nd District, whose budgets increased by P1.68 billion and P1.65 billion, respectively, in the House-approved budget compared to the NEP.
Also in the top ten are DPWH district offices which serve the constituencies of:

items: Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.58 billion)
House Speaker Bojie Dy (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.52 billion)
House appropriations chair Mika Suansing (budget of DPWH district office she shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.15 billion)
Isabela 1st District Representative Tonypet Albano (DPWH district office’s budget increased by P1.08 billion)
Isabela 3rd District Representative Ian Paul Dy (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P993 million)

blocks.caption: Summary from BetterGov.ph

blocks.text: The changes in the budget introduced by the House are not yet final, as the Senate may either approve or reject the amendments.
Any differences in the budget bills they pass would be reconciled in the bicameral conference committee. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Who is Giovanni Lopez, Marcos' new DPWH chief?
articles.summary: Atty. Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez will take the helm of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), a year after serving as secretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr).

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 2:26pm
Atty. Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez will take the helm of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), a year after serving as secretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr).
Malacañang announced Monday that Lopez would swap positions with outgoing DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon in a move supposedly aimed at "accelerating reforms and improving public service."

A lawyer and certified public accountant, Lopez was tasked by Marcos to “strengthen safeguards and institutionalize the reforms, turning them into rules, processes and systems that will keep serving Filipinos,” Malacañang said.
As the new DPWH chief, Lopez is also expected to accelerate the implementation of government infrastructure projects, including roads and bridges.
To recall, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. designated Lopez as acting transportation secretary in August 2025, amid a Cabinet revamp triggered by the flood control controversy.

Before his appointment as DOTr chief, Lopez served as the agency’s senior undersecretary for Administration, Finance and Procurement. In 2022, he also served as executive director of the Land Transportation Office (LTO).

In 2021, Lopez served as officer-in-charge executive director of the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB), while concurrently serving as undersecretary for Finance and chief of staff to then-Transportation Secretary Arthur Tugade.
Lopez was appointed director for Legal Service in 2017 before serving as assistant secretary for Procurement and Project Implementation that same year.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ube is worth $595M globally. Why is Philippines capturing just $3 million?
articles.summary: Philippine ube varieties are spreading to overseas growers who are outpacing the country in meeting global demand.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 2:25pm

MANILA, Philippines — Citing the spread of Philippine ube varieties abroad, the head of a national ube industry group has called on the Department of Agriculture to strictly enforce the suspension on fresh purple yam exports.
Chester Velasco, president of the United Ube PH Federation, said neighboring countries have been acquiring fresh ube and cultivating the crop themselves.

"As of 2025, the global valuation is around $595 million, and our share is only $3 million. We're not the number one exporter of ube. That's the sad reality," Chester Velasco, president of the United Ube PH Federation, said on One News' "The Big Story" on Saturday, October 24.
Velasco also described attempts at what he called "food fraud," where ube grown in other countries is marketed as products of the Philippines.
"There are also instances where they market it as Philippine ube even if it was locally grown in China or Vietnam," Velasco said.
For Velasco, the export restriction, which applies only to fresh ube, should effectively counter smuggling. Processed products such as ube powder, extract and halaya may still be exported.
"They should be stricter in implementing the ban because, as you said, it's so easy to smuggle," he said.
These concerns come as global demand for the crop grows while local farmers face limited access to planting materials, making it difficult for the Philippine industry to keep pace.
The United States was the biggest market for Philippine ube products, accounting for nearly half of the country's exports that year.
China and Vietnam, however, have also expanded their own production to meet the demand, Velasco said.

"Unfortunately, our neighboring countries, like China and Vietnam, have been importing fresh ube and growing it. This is what they have been doing. Vietnam has really been aggressive in growing and producing ube," Velasco said.

To support its production in the Philippines, the U.S. Department of Agriculture recently announced a development award of $34.1 million. Implemented by US-based organization TechnoServe, the fund is expected to support 12,500 Filipino ube farmers over the next five years.
The project also complements a separate P300-million government initiative to expand production by doubling crop planting areas.
Struggle with planting materials, low prices
The lack of planting materials remains one of the industry's biggest constraints. These include seedlings, tubers, setts and tissue-cultured planting materials, Velasco said.
He explained that some farmers sell their entire harvest instead of setting aside portions of ube tubers for propagation, further constraining the next planting cycle.
The industry is also dealing with uneven access to buyers.
In Romblon, Velasco said the federation encountered farmers selling ube for as little as P20 to P40 per kilo, discouraging some from planting again.
To address this, the group is promoting contract-growing arrangements that assure farmers of buyers and agreed prices.
"When there's a sudden change, we stick with that price. When the price goes up, we can negotiate. But when it goes down, we don't reduce it," Velasco said.
He said the arrangement gives farmers greater certainty that their harvest will be bought and encourages them to continue planting.
The industry also needs to improve production standards and certifications to meet export-market requirements, including organic, halal, HACCP and good manufacturing practice standards, Velasco said.

The federation, formed about three months ago, brings together farmers, growers, processors, manufacturers, exporters, academe and government agencies in an effort to consolidate what Velasco described as a fragmented ube industry.

articles.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
articles.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.

blocks.text: Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.
"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."
He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.
He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.
Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.
"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

articles.title: Who is Vince Dizon, the returning DOTr chief?
articles.summary: Malacañang announced Monday that Vince Dizon will once again lead the Department of Transportation, a little over a year after he left the office to serve at the Department of Public Works and…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:31pm

Malacañang announced Monday that Vince Dizon will once again lead the Department of Transportation (DOTr), a little over a year after he left the office to serve at the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
Dizon first served in the Cabinet of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. in February 2025, when he was appointed as DOTr secretary, succeeding Jaime Bautista.
At the DOTr, Dizon was tasked by the President to enhance physical connectivity and make life easier for the commuting public.
Six months after, at the height of the investigation into the flood control scandal, Dizon was transferred to head the DPWH, following the resignation of Manuel Bonoan.

When he moved to the DPWH, he was ordered by the President to conduct a full organizational sweep of the agency and ensure that public funds were used solely for infrastructure projects in the country.
Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Secretary Lino Cayetano said that at the DPWH, Dizon was able to disrupt a system “that had protected waste and corruption for years.”
With this, Cayetano said thousands of projects have now been open to the public, and long-unfinished projects are now being completed.

Now that he is set to return to lead DOTr, Malacañang said that Dizon is expected anew to make the daily commute of Filipinos a little easier, as well as shorten the lines and get rid of the fixers at the Land Transportation Office.
Dizon was likewise tasked by the President to push the completion of critical mass transport projects, “so workers and students spend less time on the road and more time with their families.”
Before he joined Marcos’ Cabinet, Dizon was a key figure during the administration of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
He served as president and CEO of the Bases and Conversion Development Authority (BCDA) from 2016 to 2021.

He was also the deputy chief implementer of the National Task Force Against COVID-19 during the previous administration, and was the presidential adviser on flagship programs and projects. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman to create budget watch team, study SC ruling on 2024, 2025 budgets
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will create a team to look into current budget proceedings as well as the Supreme Court"s (SC) ruling that declared as unconstitutional the General…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:28pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will create a team to look into current budget proceedings as well as the Supreme Court’s (SC) ruling that declared as unconstitutional the General Approrpations Act (GAA) for 2024 and 2025.

“Kaya nga ngayon we are starting the budget watch, pinapanood na natin iyan which didn’t happen before and dito with the decision, we will appoint a group, compose a group that will study the SC decision and the budgets that came with the decision,” Remulla said in an ambush interview.

(That’s why we are now starting the budget watch, monitoring it, which didn’t happen before. And in connection with the decision, we will appoint a group that will study the SC decision and the budgets that came with it.)
This came after the SC declared as unconstitutional the 2024 and 2025 GAAs due to budget increases made by Congress while it declared unconstitutional provisions under the 2026 GAA.
The SC also said that while the doctrine of operative fact applies, it does not shield authors, proponents, or implementors from criminal, civil, or administrative liability.
When asked about whether SC’s remark regarding the authors and implementors may lead to the President being held accountable, Remulla said that the action occurs inside Congress.

“Ang Presidente kasi just submits the bill, the proposed bill to Congress, the action goes on inside Congress and it’s very hard to follow the action, may kani-kaniyang tyempo sila eh especially those who are scheming, to add things and subtract things,” Remulla said.

(The President just submits the bill, the proposed bill, to Congress. The action takes place inside Congress, and it’s very hard to follow what happens because they each have their own timing, especially those who are scheming to add things and subtract things.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Former RAAF pilot who allegedly murdered wife was ‘love rat’ and ‘master manipulator’, jury hears
articles.summary:
Robert John Crawford on trial after wife found near ride-on lawnmower on their Toowoomba property

A former RAAF pilot was a “love rat” and “master manipulator” who staged his wife’s death…

blocks.text: A former RAAF pilot was a “love rat” and “master manipulator” who staged his wife’s death to make it appear a tragic accident, a jury has heard.
Robert John Crawford, 49, pleaded not guilty on Monday to murdering his wife Frances Elizabeth Crawford at Upper Lockyer on 29 July, 2024.
Her body was found near a ride-on lawnmower at the bottom of a retaining wall on their sprawling rural property west of Toowoomba.
Crawford murdered his wife in the context of a long relationship breakdown, prosecutor Chris Cook told a Brisbane supreme court jury.
The husband then embarked on a long campaign to make her death appear an accident, Cook alleged.
Four women with whom Crawford allegedly had affairs are due to be called as witnesses.
“He made out to be a man with good Christian values,” Cook said.
“However, his story did not match his behaviour.
“He was a man who lived a double life for a long time.”
Cook described Crawford as “a cheater, adulterer, love rat, philanderer and womaniser”.
The jury was told Crawford was not committed to the marriage, with the couple on the verge of divorce when the victim died.
The members were told Crawford was motivated to kill his wife because he stood to lose financially in a divorce settlement.
He wanted to retain possession of the couple’s house and did not want to split his superannuation.
The jury was told Crawford wavered between divorcing her husband and giving him the chance to prove himself to her and their children.
She had set her husband a detailed list of boundaries, including “deal breakers” that would lead to divorce.
The deal breakers included sexual or emotional infidelities, porn and masturbation, the court was told.
Justice Lincoln Crowley told the jury the prosecution would allege Crawford caused his wife’s death either by strangulation or blunt-force trauma.
The jury will be taken to the site of the alleged murder on Wednesday.
Justice Lincoln Crowley told the jury the viewing would help them to understand the evidence.
The trial is expected to hear from up to 47 witnesses over the next three weeks.
Crawford’s defence barrister has not yet delivered an opening statement.

articles.title: JSCC, Ombudsman team up to intensify fight vs. corruption
articles.summary: The Justice Sector Coordinating Council (JSCC) and the Office of the Ombudsman on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to strengthen interagency cooperation and address systemic delays…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:22pm

The Justice Sector Coordinating Council (JSCC) and the Office of the Ombudsman on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to strengthen interagency cooperation and address systemic delays in the fight against corruption.
The MOU was signed by Supreme Court Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, SC Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh and Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez.

In a speech, Gesmundo said the partnership would strengthen the justice system’s collective efforts to fight corruption by aligning the Ombudsman’s mandate with those of other justice sector agencies.
“We now enter a new phase, one that brings the fight against corruption more deliberately into our collective efforts to strengthen the criminal justice system,” he said.

“That is why our partnership with the Ombudsman is groundbreaking. The Ombudsman’s constitutional mandate to investigate and prosecute erring public officers complements the respective mandates of the JSCC agencies,” Gesmundo added.
The JSCC is composed of the Supreme Court (SC), the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).

According to Gesmundo, the agreement commits the parties to closer coordination, responsible information-sharing, policy development, capacity-building and efforts to address corruption-related cases and systemic challenges.
Meanwhile, Singh stressed that reforming the justice system requires collective action.
“No man or woman can change the system alone,” she said.
“Anyone who promises our people that he can change the system on his own is lying. He will fail. Because it takes an entire sector. And that is why we have the JSCC,” she added.
Remulla said his office sought to join the council's coordination mechanism as an active and contributing partner rather than merely as an observer.

Through the partnership, the Ombudsman sees opportunities to strengthen corruption prevention, address bottlenecks in corruption-related cases, improve secure information-sharing and digital systems, and build institutional capabilities to combat increasingly sophisticated forms of corruption, he said.

“Let me also be clear that cooperation does not diminish institutional independence. The Office of the Ombudsman will continue to exercise its constitutional mandate independently, just as every member of the JSCC must discharge its responsibilities,” Remulla said.
“Institutional independence and meaningful cooperation are not contradictory. They reinforce each other,” he added.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Labour urged to plug predicted £400m shortfall in overseas aid funding in 2027
articles.summary:
Official forecast indicates shortfall below 0.3% of national income in promised official development assistance

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on…

blocks.text: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
after newsletter promotion
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

articles.title: Birthkeeper who allegedly ‘groomed’ pregnant women to fear hospital could face criminal charges
articles.summary:
Victorian coroner hears Emily Lal told Stacey Warnecke that her ‘condition and mindset’ needed to be ‘solid’ to avoid a hospital birth

A birthkeeper who allegedly “groomed” pregnant women to…

blocks.text: A birthkeeper who allegedly “groomed” pregnant women to fear hospital could be referred to prosecutors to face potential criminal charges, a Victorian coroner has heard.

Stacey Warnecke died in September 2025 at Frankston hospital in Melbourne after giving birth at home and suffering a postpartum haemorrhage with birthkeeper Emily Lal by her side, having paid her $6,000 to support her throughout pregnancy.
Birthkeepers have no clinical training and operate outside the medical system.
The inquest into Warnecke’s death began in June, but closing submissions to coroner Therese McCarthy were delayed after a forensic analysis of Warnecke’s phone.

Hearings resumed on Monday, when Rachel Ellyard, in her role as counsel assisting the coroner, said that the completed analysis had revealed numerous messages, including in a group chat on the platform WhatsApp coordinated by Lal for women who were choosing freebirth. A phone call between Warnecke, a 30-year-old nutritionist and wellness influencer, and Lal was played to the court.

Ellyard said the phone evidence directly contradicted evidence from Lal, given in June, that she was hired by Warnecke primarily to play the role of a supportive friend, and that the money paid to her was primarily for her time, but not for medical advice.

“Ms Lal saw her role as to groom her clients into being strong enough to resist the temptation to seek medical help during labor, to seek pain relief during labor, to go to hospital during labor,” Ellyard said.

“It’s clear that Ms. Lal thought that in most cases, going to hospital would represent a failure of someone who hadn’t done the work, who hadn’t understood enough what the intensity of labor was going to be.”
During the call, Warnecke told Lal that she envisioned having a “wise woman” next to her during her first childbirth, to guide her when asking: “Am I dying, or am I alright?”
Warnecke told Lal she was afraid of the hospital.
Lal responded: “You should be scared of the hospital.”
“It’s a terrifying place. For me personally, I think the biggest, the key … to actually staying home and having your baby … is that your mindset and your condition needs to be so solid.”

Lal also told Warnecke that midwives who attend home births sometimes inadvertently sabotage them, because if the birth goes on too long, they tell the woman to go to hospital. This is sometimes just because the midwife is exhausted, Lal said.
She told Warnecke: “I manage my own energy as much as I can in that way, so that I don’t subconsciously sabotage a person.”

Lal previously told the court that she was not clinically trained, and that it was not her responsibility to make Warnecke’s birth safer, or to call an ambulance unless specifically asked. Lal said she never gave Warnecke medical advice, and only shared her own experiences of freebirthing her own children.

Ellyard said on Monday that given the evidence from the call and many messages and documents obtained from Warnecke’s phone, “the role that Stacey thought Ms. Lal would play during the freebirth … was to help her by keeping her safe”.
“Stacey was placing considerable reliance on Ms. Lal, in whom she had placed considerable trust.
“Ms. Lal was an expert. She was providing advice. She was providing referrals. She was selling supplements. She was offering commentary.
“This is all quite inconsistent with the idea of just being a friend who pulls your hair back and wipes your forehead. It’s something much more structured, much more deliberate.”
Ellyard said Warnecke’s husband, Nathan, had also been “reassured or indoctrinated into a sense that his role was just to just sit back and support, and that whatever Stacey experienced was alright”.
Lal was invited to return to court to give further evidence after the phone analysis, but had declined to, the court heard.
Lal only gave evidence previously on the condition that the Coroner grant her a certificate of protection so that her evidence could not be used against her in any future proceedings.

Ellyard put to the Coroner on Monday that it would be open to her to find that Lal had committed purgery “in relation to the falsity of the evidence” and to refer her to the Office of Public Prosecutions [OPP].
The OPP prepares and conducts criminal matters on behalf of the director.

“Having regard to the materials that have now become available … it would be open to your honor to form the view that Ms Lal wasn’t truthful in the evidence that she gave to you, and that a referral could be made in relation to the offence of perjury,” Ellyard said.

She said there was also evidence Lal had been “holding herself out as someone capable of giving such expert advice and capable of meeting the needs of pregnant women in a range of circumstances” despite having no authority.

The court previously heard that Lal had asked Warnecke three times whether she wanted an ambulance called after she gave birth to the placenta, lost up to 1.5 litres of blood, then began struggling to breathe.
Lal previously told the court that it was not her role to call an ambulance against her client’s wishes, even if the woman was unconscious and dying.
Warnecke said yes to an ambulance the third time, but by the time paramedics arrived she was seriously unwell, having suffered a massive postpartum haemorrhage.
Warnecke died in hospital several hours later from related complications, with the hospital exhausting its blood supply trying to save her.
Ellyard said on Monday: “Stacey would have survived if she was in hospital”.

Midwives and doctors know that postpartum haemorrhage is the most common complication of childbirth and are so well trained to identify it and treat it that “women do not die in hospital” from it in well-resourced countries, Ellyard said.
Warnecke also “would have survived if she was giving birth at home with a registered midwife,” Ellyard said, drawing from evidence given by medical professionals earlier in the inquest.
“She suffered a known complication of childbirth, which was eminently treatable if identified and responded to immediately.”
The coroner will deliver her findings at a later date.

articles.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
articles.summary: Andre McKechnie, who murdered a property developer, argued it was his right to enjoy Australian culture.

blocks.text: A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.
Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.
And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.
McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.
During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.
The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.
A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.
The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.

It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

articles.title: Old playbook vs Duterte critics resurfaces in journalist Philip Lustre's arrest
articles.summary: "They couldn’t find him" to serve the complaint, but police found him when it was time to arrest him.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 11:54am

MANILA, Philippines — The weekend arrest of journalist Philip Lustre Jr. followed methods long used to harass former President Rodrigo Duterte's critics, his lawyer said, pointing to a complaint filed far from where the accused lives and timing the arrest to block immediate bail.
Lawyer Dino de Leon, counsel for the 72-year-old, noted the "highly irregular" steps in the cyber libel case initiated against Lustre in Davao City, the political stronghold of the Duterte family.

Among others, De Leon flagged how Lustre did not learn of the charges against him until police arrived with a warrant for him in the middle of a forum on Saturday, October 24. De Leon, who was attending the forum as guest speaker, stepped in to represent him.
Denial of due process
De Leon said the prosecutor’s subpoena for the preliminary investigation was sent to a wrong address, depriving Lustre of his right to submit a counter-affidavit before the court ordered his arrest.
"Hindi siya mahanap, hindi siya matunton. Pero pagka-posas na, ang daling matunton," De Leon said in an interview with DZMM on Monday, October 26.
(They could not find him or track him down [for the subpoena]. But when it came time to handcuff him, he was easy to locate.)
De Leon criticized prosecutors for bypassing preliminary notice and argued that presenting an arrest warrant as a first notice violates basic constitutional protections.

"Hindi naman puwedeng posas ang una mong makikita," De Leon said. "May preliminary investigation, eh mali 'yung address... So pagdating sa subpoena para ma-make sure na may due process, na-depensa niya sarili niya, makapag-file ng counter-affidavit — wala."

(You cannot just present handcuffs first. There should be a preliminary investigation, but the address was wrong. So when it came to serving the subpoena to ensure due process and allow him to defend himself—nothing.)
He called on the Department of Justice to investigate whether Davao City prosecutors are routinely skirting the regular process to swiftly act on complaints by the Duterte family.

"Nananawagan kami sa Department of Justice na imbestigahan kung kalakaran ba ito sa Davao City Prosecutor's Office," he said. "Basta mga Duterte o mga Davao group ang nagrereklamo, wala nang due process?"

(We are calling on the Department of Justice to investigate whether this is standard practice in the Davao City Prosecutor's Office. Whenever the Dutertes or the Davao group file a complaint, is due process discarded?)
Calculated weekend arrest

Judge Retrina Fuentes of the Davao City Regional Trial Court Branch 10 signed the warrant on October 2. It charges Lustre with online libel under Section 4(c)(4) of the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.
Police served the warrant on a Saturday morning when court offices were closed and processing bail would've been more difficult.
Lustre, a senior citizen who has difficulty walking, was held for hours and was unable to eat lunch while his legal team scrambled to secure his release, De Leon said.
Defense lawyers eventually located an emergency duty night judge late Saturday evening to process his P48,000 bail, allowing Lustre to avoid staying in detention through the weekend.
In a social media post after his release, Lustre called the arrest “a special operation” against him.
“The intention was to have me arrested on a Saturday and stay in jail on a weekend because I might not be able to post bail for my release,” Lustre wrote.
Police officers unable to explain warrant
De Leon also flagged the lack of knowledge by the arresting officers themselves who could not explain who had filed the complaint against Lustre.
While the warrant specified the offense as cyber libel, it omitted the private complainant's identity and specific facts.

De Leon explained that under the court system, warrants uploaded to the electronic e-warrant portal often lack attached case information. This leaves police officers unable to explain the basis of an arrest, as was the case on Saturday.
“Dapat sana in-upload ‘yung information para pag tinanong naman ‘yung pulis, ‘Bakit n’yo po ako inaaresto?’ eh may maisagot naman ‘yung pulis,” he said.
(The information should have been uploaded so that when the police are asked, “Why are you arresting me?”, they would have an answer.)
"'Di ba nagmumukhang katawa-tawa yung ating buong sistema, na 'gagawin lang po namin trabaho namin wala kaming kaalam-alam'?" he added.
(Doesn't our entire system look ridiculous — with the stance, 'We’re just doing our jobs; we have no idea about anything'?)
Filing venue
The complaint was filed in Davao City, nearly 1,000 kilometers from Manila, where Lustre is based.
Under the Revised Penal Code, a private individual may file a libel case where the material was first printed and published, or where he or she lived when it was published.
Lustre is the author of “Kill, Kill, Kill,” a book on killings during Duterte’s drug war.
Duterte is on trial at the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity over the drug war he carried out as president, and earlier, as Davao mayor.
Under Duterte
Duterte often attacked news organizations that reported critically on his drug war.
In December 2019, Duterte vowed to see to it that broadcaster ABS-CBN went off the air, a promise that his allies in the House delivered by 2020, when they rejected the network’s franchise renewal.

News site Rappler and its chief executive, Maria Ressa, also faced a string of criminal cases under Duterte. Ressa was arrested at her office one evening in February 2019, too late to post bail, and spent the night in custody.
She was convicted of cyber libel in 2020 and has appealed the case to the Supreme Court.
Media groups have long pushed for the decriminalization of libel in the country, where several such cases have been used to intimidate the press.

A United Nations special rapporteur has also backed calls to repeal the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, a highly contested law that rights groups say has been weaponized to go after critics of government.

articles.title: Thorough, objective probe into fatal PAF plane crash ongoing --DND
articles.summary: The Department of National Defense said Monday that a thorough and objective investigation is being conducted into the fatal crash that resulted in the death of four pilots during a training flight…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 11:48am

The Department of National Defense said Monday that a thorough and objective investigation is being conducted into the fatal plane crash that resulted in the death of four pilots during a training flight over Fernando Air Base in Lipa City, Batangas.

"An investigation is ongoing and will be conducted thoroughly and objectively to establish the facts, determine the causes, and identify any gaps that require corrective action and prevent similar tragedies," the DND said in a statement.
"The DND remains committed to transparency, accountability, and ensuring the safety of our personnel," it added.
It said it mourns the tragic loss of four Philippine Air Force pilots in the SF-260 aircraft accident.

"We extend our heartfelt condolences to their grieving families, loved ones, friends, and fellow airmen and women who share in this profound loss. Their service and sacrifice for the nation will not be forgotten," the DND said.
The incident happened at 3:51 p.m. on Friday, October 23.
Two single-propeller SF-260 aircraft were involved, with both of them going down within the base perimeter.
Video footage obtained by GMA News showed the two aircraft colliding in midair. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Vince Dizon, Giovanni Lopez trade posts at DOTr, DPWH
articles.summary: Dizon is back to fix Filipinos' commute, while Lopez is tasked to sustain DPWH reforms.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 11:05am
Composite image shows file photo of Cabinet officials Giovanni Lopez and Vince Dizon.
PCO, file; Philstar.com composite
This is a developing report. Please check back for more details.

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has switched the heads of the transportation and public works departments, sending Vince Dizon back to lead his former agency and Giovanni Lopez taking his place.
Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano announced the changes at a press briefing Monday, October 26.
Dizon will return to the Department of Transportation, while Lopez, who had been serving as acting transportation secretary, has been appointed to lead the Department of Public Works and Highways.

"In the president's own words: 'We are shifting gears to accelerate reform. Secretary Dizon goes to DOTr to fix the daily commute. Secretary Lopez goes to DPWH to make sure the reforms there last,'" Cayetano said.

"Lahat ng ito, para lalong bumilis at gumaan ang serbisyo ng gobyerno para sa ating mga kababayan," he added. ("All of this is to make government services faster and easier for our fellow Filipinos.")

The appointments reverse a Cabinet reshuffle made in August 2025. Dizon, then transportation secretary, was appointed to lead the DPWH on Aug. 31, 2025, following the resignation of then-Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan amid controversy over alleged anomalous flood control projects.
Lopez, then a DOTr undersecretary, was appointed acting transportation secretary to take over the post vacated by Dizon.

articles.title: Outsource Philippine visas? Ombudsman call draws DFA defense of mandate
articles.summary: DFA pushes back against Boying Remulla's call to outsource processing to third parties.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 10:43am

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla responds to senators’ questions regarding the Philippines’ residual obligations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) following its withdrawal from the tribunal, during a public hearing on Thursday, April 10, 2025.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called for Philippine visa processing to be outsourced to third-party providers, a comment which drew a sharp objection from the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Speaking on DZRH on Saturday, October 24, Remulla said foreign service officers should focus on diplomacy rather than handling visa applications.
"Ang problema ng DFA, they forget that their primary job is to be diplomats. Eh dito iba 'yung gusto nilang mangyari, gusto nilang magnegosyo," Remulla said.
("The problem with the DFA is that they forget that their primary job is to be diplomats. But here, they want something else to happen; they want to go into business.")

"Ako talaga ang stance ko diyan, let the Philippine visa processing be done by a third party, VFS (Visa Facilitation Services). Para alam natin kung sino pumapasok, nave-vet natin lahat ng pumapasok," he added.
("My position is to let Philippine visa processing be handled by a third party, like VFS. That way, we know who is entering and we can vet everyone coming in.")
Remulla argued that using a third-party provider would establish a uniform international standard for processing applications and screening tourists and business travelers.
"Kasi pag binigay sa VFS 'yan, it will become a standard of the country for the rest of the world," he said.
("Because if that is given to VFS, it will become the country's standard for the rest of the world.")
Remulla also said immigration matters should pass through the Department of Justice because of the need to conduct background checks on people entering the country.
"Dapat dumaan sa Department of Justice yan. I think so, because we want to get a background of the people entering our country," Remulla said.
("That should go through the Department of Justice. I think so, because we want to get a background check on the people entering our country.")
DFA 'strongly objects'
The DFA pushed back against Remulla's remarks, saying they undermined the agency's integrity and unfairly tarnished the reputation of the Philippine Foreign Service and its personnel.
The department said its authority to issue visas is grounded in both domestic and international law.
It cited Executive Order No. 292, or the Administrative Code of 1987, which recognizes visa issuance as a consular function, as well as the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations.
The DFA also explained that third-party providers such as VFS may perform administrative functions, including receiving visa applications, but do not have the authority to approve or deny them.
That authority remains with Philippine diplomatic missions, the department said.

"The visa fees collected are pursuant to applicable laws and regulations, including the prescribed Schedule of Fees. The DFA does not tolerate corruption and remains committed to accountability, transparency, and utmost professionalism in the delivery of public service," the DFA said. — with reports from Alyana Uy
